label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
# The last of the 4am toast

On Saturday I did my last night shift. 21:00 to 07:30, majors, a Saturday in November, which is about as honest a send-off as the job could give me. From Monday I'm on the days-only rota. After fourteen years of nights, that's it.

I've tried to write this about six times since spring, when it first became clear this was coming. Every version turned into a eulogy, as if someone had died, or a long complaint about the NHS, and I've written enough of those to last everyone a lifetime. This isn't about staffing. It's just about nights, and what they were like, and what they did to me, good and bad.

The practical reasons are boring. My knees aren't what they were. My sleep has been in pieces for years. And at my last check-up the GP looked at my blood pressure, looked at me, and said in the tone GPs save for doctors who should know better that it was "not a joke anymore." So I'm moving. It was my decision and it was the right one, and I'll come back to that.

## The first winter

My first night shift was in 2012, as an SHO. I don't remember much about the shift itself. I remember a morning a few weeks into that first winter, sitting in my car in the car park at the Infirmary and crying because I couldn't remember whether I'd given someone their second dose.

I had. I'd checked, and I'd written it down, and I went back in and checked again anyway. But for twenty minutes in that car I was absolutely convinced I'd hurt someone, and there was nobody to ring at that hour who wouldn't think I'd lost it. I can still see the frost on the windscreen, those little fern patterns, and the orange of the car park lights coming through them.

I think about that version of me a lot. She was very tired and very frightened and she didn't know yet that the fear wouldn't go away, but that she'd learn to carry it. That's most of what nights taught me.

## What nights are actually like

People who haven't worked them think nights are all adrenaline. Blue lights, crash calls, the sort of thing that ends up on television. Some of that happens. But mostly nights are about something much less dramatic. They're about staying kind at five in the morning when you've got nothing left.

Five o'clock is the worst hour. Not three, as everyone assumes. At three you're still running on whatever got you through the evening. By five it's all gone, the windows are still black, and the patient in front of you is frightened and in pain and has every right to your full attention. You give it to them anyway, from somewhere. I don't know where it comes from. I've never been able to explain it to anyone who hasn't done it, and I've stopped trying.

Nights are also where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers about, fewer meetings, fewer people walking through with lanyards and clipboards. What's left is the work and the people doing it. Things get said more plainly at night. People are more honest about what they don't know. And people are kinder, I think because everyone knows how thin they're stretched and so nobody pretends otherwise. You'd be surprised how much gentleness there is in a busy majors at 4am.

## The toast

Speaking of 4am. Someone always makes toast in the staff room at four. It's happened on every night shift I can remember, in every department I've worked in on nights. You come off the floor for five minutes and the smell's already there and there's a plate of it on the side, cut into triangles, sometimes buttered, sometimes with a jar of jam left open next to it.

Nobody ever admits to starting it. I've asked. Everyone says it was already there when they came in. I've come to believe it simply makes itself, like something out of a folk tale, as long as there are enough tired people in the building who need it.

## Folasade

Our charge nurse on nights is Folasade. She has done nights for twenty-two years, eight more than me, and she still beats me up the stairs. Every time. She doesn't even do it on purpose, she just goes, and by the time I've reached the landing she's already talking to someone and has sorted out whatever I was coming up to ask about.

A lot of what I know about staying kind at 5am, I learned from watching her. She's not soft. She'll tell a junior doctor exactly what she thinks of their plan. But I've never once seen her be unkind to a patient, however late it is, however rude they've been, however many times they've asked the same question. She makes it look easy. I know it isn't.

## What they gave me

Some of the moments that have stayed with me are the smallest ones. Last winter, about three in the morning, an elderly man held my hand while I was examining him and told me I had his daughter's hands. That was it. He didn't say any more and I didn't ask. He went home three days later. I've thought about it more than almost anything else that happened that year.

I don't think that would've happened at three in the afternoon. Not because people are different in the day, but because the night takes something away, all the noise and the bustle and the pretending, and what's left is quieter and closer. People say things at night they wouldn't say otherwise. Sometimes it's frightening, sometimes it's funny, and sometimes it's an old man telling you that you remind him of someone he loves.

## What they took

They took plenty, and I don't want to pretend they didn't.

They took my sleep, obviously, and probably some years off my blood pressure. They took weekends and birthdays and a fair number of friendships that couldn't survive me never being free on a Saturday night.

They also took both of my nieces' naming ceremonies. I watched both of them on a video call, once from a car park and once from my kitchen with blackout blinds down in the middle of the afternoon, while my sister and the whole family were together in Bangalore. My sister has never once complained about this. Not once, in all these years. She just sends me the photos and the videos and tells me who asked after me. If you're reading this: thank you. I noticed. I always noticed.

## Sunday morning

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road with the sun coming up. I had the shipping forecast on catch-up, which I've done for years on the drive home, all those names that mean nothing to me and everything at the same time. Dogger, Fisher, German Bight. And somewhere around the station it occurred to me that I wouldn't see that light from this side again. Not like this, coming off a shift, with the night behind me and everyone else's day just starting.

That's when it got me, really. Not the last handover, not the goodbyes. The light on the London Road.

## The traitor bit

Here's the thing I've been struggling to say. I'm relieved. I am properly, deeply relieved. I'm going to sleep at night. I'm going to see daylight on my days off without feeling like I've stolen it. My body is going to stop being cross with me.

And I feel like a traitor for being relieved. For leaving the night team. For leaving Folasade on the stairs. For deciding that my knees and my blood pressure matter, when the people I've worked alongside for years are still going to be there on Saturday night, and the Saturday after that.

I know that's not quite fair on myself. Everyone who's said anything to me has said some version of "about time." But I think it's possible to know a decision is right and still grieve it a bit. I'm letting myself do both.

## Saturday night

So this Saturday, at about four in the morning, I'll be asleep. Actually asleep, in a bed, in the dark, like a normal person.

And down at the department, someone will come off the floor for five minutes and find the smell already there and a plate on the side, cut into triangles. Folasade will be first up the stairs. The night will be doing what it always does, quietly, and mostly without anyone noticing.

The toast will still be there. It doesn't need me to make it. It never did.
